newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds seen carving out more gains as '97 starts.
newsitem.headline: Bunds seen carving out more gains as '97 starts.

text.p: Frankfurt, Dec 30 - Bunds are likely to continue their recent solid rally early next year with economic fundamentals here and in the U.S. giving investors reason to increase fixed-income holdings, analysts said on Monday.

Experts said even with uncertainty about the impact of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the yield on the benchmark 10-year Bund should move toward 5.50 percent or lower in the first few months of 1997 from around 5.78 percent now.
"It is not over yet," said David Brown, economist at Bear Stearns in London. "We are entering the final furlong of what has been a steady rally."
Analysts said the same cocktail of low interest rates, inflation and growth -- both in the U.S. and in Germany -- should give investors reason to buy Bunds.
The most actively traded DTB Bund futures contract, for example, has climbed to 100.84 at Monday's close from 97.18 at the end of August.
"The outlook is pretty favourable," said Christoph Anhamm, bond market analyst at UBS in Frankfurt.
With the U.S. market the world's largest bond market and Bunds closely following their American counterparts of late, events in the U.S. can be as important as those in Germany.
Analysts said the normal hazard that faces the Bund market early in given year is profit-taking from investors who want to lock in gains.
But investors have been noticeably lacking during the market's recent gains, offering limited scope for profit-taking.
"There is limited risk for institutional profit-taking," one bond trader in Frankfurt said.
Analysts said the spectre of EMU also poses little immediate risk to Bunds.

Speculation that monetary union will happen on schedule in 1999 has helped improve the overall European bond market through so-called convergence plays -- buying high-yielding bonds of countries like Italy and Spain on the anticipation they will qualify for EMU.
But even if investors should grow more sceptical about EMU and sell those markets, they may opt to park the proceeds in the perceived safety of German debt markets, lifting Bunds still higher.

German debt probably will not be able to break out of its range this year relative to Treasury notes, however. Analysts said they see the spread between benchmark ten-year Bunds and T-notes, now around 60 basis ponts, moving to 70 basis points.
But that will likely be the limit and the spread could well start to narrow back toward 50 basis points later in the year, especially amid signs that the U.S. economy may pick up.
Analysts also said they see the Bund yield curve continuing to flatten as it becomes clearer that the Bundesbank will not cut interest rates much futher.
One analyst said he saw the spread between five and 10-year notes narrowing to around 80 basis points from around 93 basis points now.
